newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean lawmakers want Tokyo apology for seizure.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean lawmakers want Tokyo apology for seizure.

text.p: Three South Korean members of parliament went to Japan on Tuesday to demand an apology and compensation by the Tokyo government for the seizure of five South Korean fishing boats in disputed waters.

Lawmaker Kim Young-jin of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, leader of the group, said they would seek an interview with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda during their five-day visit.
"We urge the Japanese government to apologise to the people of the Republic of Korea and compensate in full for losses caused by such illegal actions," he told reporters before leaving for Tokyo.
In the past few months, Japanese patrol boats captured five South Korean fishing vessels in waters recently claimed by Tokyo.

The lawmakers' visit follows numerous anti-Japanese protests in South Korea and a resolution adopted last month by the National Assembly, which denounced Japan for the seizures and called for the immediate release of a detained captain.
All five boats and the crew members have been released except for the captain of one of them.
The lawmakers are also due to interview the detained captain, Kim Soon-ki, and meet Japanese members of parliament to deliver the Seoul National Assembly resolution.

"It is a clearly an illegal act to abduct our fishing boats based on the unilateral implementation of a straight baseline to define territorial waters, which breaks international laws and a fisheries agreement between South Korea and Japan," the delegation leader said.

Last month, South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Lee Ki-choo called in the Japanese ambassador in Seoul, Shintaro Yamashita, to lodge a formal protest over the seizures, and protesters burned Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in effigy.

Japan and South Korea are currently negotiating over the revision of the fisheries agreement, and the two delegations are scheduled to meet for a two-day meeting on Wednesday in Tokyo, South Korea's foreign ministry said.
Japan says it expanded its territorial waters in January following a new maritime convention introduced by the United Nations in November, 1994.
Seoul argues that the existing agreement, which has been in force for more than 30 years, must be observed until a revision is worked out.
